name: Facial height / skull size theory

lead: Facial height / skull size theory is a community framework which says that how large the head is, and how tall the face is from brow to chin, set the baseline against which every other feature is judged. Members use it to describe why two people with similar features can look very different, and to decide which proportions are worth working on.

The terms have two meanings online. 'Skull size' refers to overall head circumference and frame, sometimes called 'skull mogging' when a larger head makes someone look more imposing beside another person. 'Face height' usually means the vertical length of the face, though threads also use 'face vs height' to compare facial attractiveness with body height. Clinical research measures facial height in orthodontics and sleep medicine, but it has not been used to test the forum theory directly.

paras: In practice people compare photos and measurements of head size or face length, then choose ways to balance them: hairstyles and facial hair that add or reduce visual length, framing choices, and for some, orthodontic or jaw-surgery consultations that change vertical proportions. Discussions are mostly photo comparisons rather than protocols.

The framework itself carries no physical risk, but forum posts describe distress when members compare their measurements to others. Procedures sometimes discussed in connection with it, such as jaw or orbital osteotomies, are major surgery with the usual surgical risks and are decided with a surgeon. Orthodontic literature stresses that facial height changes are assessed individually.

angle.text: Proponents use the idea as a map of which proportions stand out in a face. Hairstyle, beard and framing choices are the low-intervention ways people adjust perceived length, while orthodontics and jaw surgery are the clinical routes some members research.

lead: Facial height / skull size theory is a framework from looksmaxxing forums. It holds that two broad dimensions, the size of the skull and the vertical height of the face, work as a baseline for attractiveness and presence, with individual features such as the eyes, nose and jaw read relative to that baseline. People use it to understand why some faces look more proportional than others and to decide what to adjust: hairstyle volume and length, facial hair, framing, and for some members, orthodontic or surgical consultation.

In the way members use the terms, 'skull size' covers head circumference and cranial width, and 'skull mogging' describes one person's larger head making another look smaller beside them [1]. 'Face height' covers the vertical length of the face, from hairline or brow to chin, with a long lower third being the version most often discussed [2]. Some threads use 'face vs height' to ask whether facial attractiveness or body height matters more socially [3][4].

Published research does not test the forum theory as stated. Facial height is a standard measurement in orthodontics, craniofacial surgery and sleep medicine, where researchers examine how mouth breathing, airway obstruction and jaw position relate to vertical facial growth [5][6][7][8]. Separately, psychologists have studied facial proportions, including the width-to-height ratio of the face and the spacing of eyes and mouth, in relation to perceived attractiveness and dominance [9][10][11].

paras: The framework treats skull size and face height as base-level traits. A forum thread titled 'skull size is everything irl' states the strong version, while others argue the reverse; both sides appear in the community [12][13].

Face height is discussed in several ways: the height of the face relative to its width, the length of the lower third, and the contrast with body height. One member describes planning an orbital box osteotomy with tripod osteotomies in order to change facial height-to-width ratio and palpebral fissure length [14].

The vocabulary is shared with the rest of the PSL and 'pheno' culture, in which a face is described by a bundle of ratios and traits rather than a single feature. Within that vocabulary, 'face height pheno' and 'frame' are treated as properties that are hard to change, which is part of why threads about them are often framed as questions of fixed versus fixable traits [2][3].

Proponents say a larger skull gives a more imposing look in side-by-side photos and in person, pointing to photos in which two people with a similar shoulder height appear to differ in head size [1]. Others say skull size is overrated, and threads such as 'skull size is cope' and 'skull size does not matter' argue that features and grooming dominate [12][15].

A frequent topic is whether face height, body height or both govern how people are treated. One member says he would rather be a very tall man than a shorter man with an actor's face, arguing that height brings a more primal respect; another thread titled 'face > height any day of the week' argues the opposite, and replies in it say face is generally more important but not by much, and that being below about 5'6" in the West is a severe handicap [4][3]. Another thread asks how much face height affects friendships and social circles [2].

Community members measure head circumference with a tape and post the figure, as in a thread asking how an unusually high measurement affects standing [16]. Clinically, facial height is measured on lateral cephalograms. Holly Broadbent introduced the cephalostat in 1931 to standardise head radiographs, and later analyses by Harvold and others define lower anterior facial height as the distance from the anterior nasal spine to menton, while Jarabak compares posterior with anterior facial height [8].

Photographic comparisons, the community's most common tool, depend on camera conditions. A 2016 PLOS ONE study of 45 people photographed at three focal lengths found that facial width-to-height ratio measured from the photos was significantly smaller at the shortest focal length, and that raters judged attractiveness, dominance and masculinity differently across the three versions of the same face [17].

Practical adjustments discussed by members are general: hairstyle length and volume, beard shape, eyewear and framing, and consultation with orthodontists or maxillofacial surgeons about jaw position.

Psychology research has examined several vertical and horizontal proportions. In a 2010 Vision Research series of four experiments, Pallett, Link and Lee altered the vertical distance between the eyes and mouth, and the eye spacing, in photographs of Caucasian female faces and had 126 mostly female students make paired attractiveness comparisons. Ratings peaked when the eye-to-mouth distance was about 36% of face length and the eye spacing about 46% of face width, values that matched averages from 40 faces; the authors list the use of only female faces and a mostly female student sample among the limitations [9].

The facial width-to-height ratio (fWHR) compares the width of the face with the height of the upper face. In a 2014 Psychological Science study at speed-dating events with over 150 participants aged 18 to 32, Valentine and colleagues reported that men with higher fWHR were rated more dominant and that women expressed more interest in them as short-term partners and were more likely to choose them for a second date, even after accounting for age and rated attractiveness; the findings are correlational [10].

A 2015 meta-analysis by Haselhuhn, Ormiston and Wong of 14 articles reported a small positive correlation between men's fWHR and aggression (r =.11, N = 4,141), stronger in laboratory studies than in field studies; the authors note that the measure explains only a small share of variance and that the study did not test whether the cause is biological or social [11].

Wikipedia's overview of physical attractiveness summarises related findings on averageness, symmetry and sexual dimorphism, including a 2008 Italian study that compared 93 casting-agency adolescents with 324 reference adolescents and found that the attractive group had, among other differences, reduced facial height and depth [18].
No studies found that test the forum theory that skull size or face height determines attractiveness. Research on facial height exists in orthodontic and airway medicine, summarised below.

A 2025 narrative review reported a strong link between mouth breathing in children and dentofacial changes such as adenoid facies, Class II malocclusion and anterior open bite, with compensatory head posture; the authors note the causal direction remains debated [6]. A 2024 review of adenoid facies describes altered facial height proportions in children with enlarged adenoids [7].

A meta-analysis of cephalometric studies found that adults with obstructive sleep apnea had, on average, longer anterior lower facial height (about 2.5 mm) and different hyoid position than controls [5]. A controlled study of growing patients with increased vertical dimension reported cephalometric changes with cervical headgear compared with controls [19].
A restorative-dentistry review states that changing occlusal vertical dimension can improve visual proportions in facial height as one part of treatment [20].

Clinicians describe excess lower facial height with the term long face syndrome, also called skeletal open bite, which is linked to vertical maxillary excess; some authors question whether it qualifies as a syndrome. In growing patients treatment aims to control lower-jaw descent, and severe cases may combine orthodontics with orthognathic surgery [21].

Orthognathic (corrective jaw) surgery is performed by oral and maxillofacial surgeons with orthodontists. Wikipedia states that a total maxilla osteotomy is used to treat long face syndrome, and describes initial healing of 2 to 6 weeks and bone remodelling over a further 2 to 4 months. Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection and nerve damage that can cause numbness, usually temporary [22].

In forum threads, members who discuss these procedures describe them as a way to change proportions that hair or grooming cannot, while others in the same community regard skull and face height as unchangeable [14][3].

Forum posts show members comparing measurements and describing anxiety about fixed traits, such as threads asking how 'over' a given skull measurement is [16]. Procedures mentioned in these discussions are surgical and carry anaesthesia, healing and revision risks; orthodontic and surgical outcomes are individual [22].

The terms sit alongside other framework vocabulary such as 'mogging' and 'frame'. Threads range from enthusiastic claims to sceptical ones, and some members tie the concept to proportion and framing rather than to a ranking [1][12][15].

lore.intro: Threads on looksmax.org debate whether skull size and face height are first-order traits or overrated, and how they compare with body height [12][13][3].

claims.claim: A bigger skull 'mogs' a smaller one
Skull size is 'cope' and does not matter
Face height matters more than body height, or the reverse
A wider, shorter face reads as more dominant or attractive
There is an ideal vertical proportion for the face
Face height can be changed surgically to alter proportions

timeline.event: Holly Broadbent introduces the cephalostat, standardising head radiographs used to measure facial height [8].
A Compendium of Continuing Education in Dentistry review discusses altering occlusal vertical dimension to improve facial proportions [20].
Pallett, Link and Lee report optimal eye-mouth and eye-spacing ratios in Vision Research [9].
Valentine and colleagues publish the speed-dating study linking facial width-to-height ratio to dominance ratings and short-term interest [10].
Haselhuhn, Ormiston and Wong publish a meta-analysis of fWHR and aggression in men [11].
A PLOS ONE study shows that focal length changes measured fWHR and ratings of the same faces [17].
A meta-analysis of cephalometric studies reports longer anterior lower facial height in adults with obstructive sleep apnea [5].
A review in Frontiers in Public Health describes adenoid facies and altered facial height proportions [7].
A narrative review links childhood mouth breathing with dentofacial changes [6].
